content: Following discharge from an Ebola Treatment Center (ETC), pregnant women should have follow-up visits scheduled every 7–10 days for the remainder of their pregnancy. Individualized counseling and education should be provided to the woman, her partner, and family. This should include information on the risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes and Ebola virus transmission, strategies to reduce transmission risks, early warning signs of complications, preparation for delivery or potential abortion, and the importance of abstinence from sexual intercourse or consistent condom use if abstinence is not feasible. In cases where home birth or spontaneous abortion is unavoidable, women should be provided with home delivery kits containing gloves, disinfectant solutions, and disposal bags. They should also receive education on the safe handling of pregnancy-related fluids and tissues using infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. Pregnant women who recover from Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) with a viable pregnancy are considered high-risk. Starting at 36 weeks of gestation, they should receive care at a facility equipped to manage obstetric procedures and implement Ebola-specific IPC measures to reduce the risk of adverse events and minimize transmission risks. Admission can be to an ETC or a similarly equipped facility. At 36 weeks, standard IPC precautions should be followed unless labor or adverse events occur. If labor or complications arise, care should be provided in Ebola-specific isolation areas (hot/red zones). If labor, rupture of membranes, or bleeding occurs, pregnant women should be transferred to a private area within the ETC capable of managing labor and potential complications. Community health workers and traditional birth attendants should be educated on the importance of these management protocols for pregnant Ebola survivors to ensure community support and understanding. Only women who conceived prior to EVD infection remain at risk for transmission after recovery and have an increased likelihood of adverse pregnancy outcomes. This understanding is critical for healthcare workers to reduce stigma and ensure adequate healthcare access for these women. Ebola-specific IPC measures should be implemented for pregnant women with acute EVD or those who have recovered but are at risk of transmitting the virus through pregnancy-related fluids and tissues during childbirth, adverse pregnancy events, or newborn care. Pregnancy-related fluids and tissues should be tested for Ebola virus using RT-PCR. Invasive obstetric procedures in pregnant women with acute EVD or following recovery should only be performed by trained and competent personnel using full personal protective equipment (PPE). The least invasive option should always be prioritized. Breastfeeding women who have recovered from EVD should have their breast milk tested for Ebola virus using RT-PCR. Breastfeeding can only resume if two consecutive negative tests, 24 hours apart, confirm the absence of the virus in breast milk. If a woman currently has acute EVD or tests positive for Ebola virus in breast milk, breastfeeding should be discontinued. If the child is an infant without safe and appropriate breast milk substitutes, separation of the mother and child should be considered. National authorities in countries with Zaire Ebola virus outbreaks should introduce the rVSV-ZEBOV-GP vaccine and offer it to pregnant women within a research framework, ensuring informed consent and a transparent, evidence-based process. Research priorities include determining the efficacy and safety of investigational therapies (e.g., REGN-EB3 and mAb114) in pregnant women with acute EVD, investigating pregnancy and neonatal outcomes, and assessing viral persistence in pregnancy-related tissues and fluids. Further research should explore the infectivity potential of breast milk in women with acute or convalescent EVD, the performance of rapid diagnostic testing in breast milk, and the relationship between positive RT-PCR results and live infectious virus in breast milk over time. Investigational therapies and vaccines should be evaluated for their ability to reduce mother-to-child transmission of Ebola virus and optimize maternal, pregnancy, and neonatal outcomes. Cultural alternatives to post-mortem cesarean delivery should be explored, and strategies to improve communication and counseling for pregnant women in the context of EVD should be developed. The impact of vaccine use on traditional IPC measures and prevention efforts should be assessed to ensure effective transmission reduction. Healthcare personnel should receive optimal training and equipment to effectively care for pregnant women with confirmed or suspected EVD. The development of these guidelines was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP/UNFPA/UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development, and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP).
